To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the simulation of n-partites Hamiltonians is NP-complete, 2) the required number of steps is at most exponential in the number of qubits, 3) the number of time is exponential in the number qubits for graphs with irrational spectrum, 4) the number of steps is linear in the number of sites in nearest-neighbor interactions on lattices

(a) for any n-partite interaction graph with rational spectrum there exists a simulation that requires O(n) time steps; (b) for any n-vertex graph with irrational spectrum there exists a Hamiltonian that requires Ω(n) time steps for any simulation; and (c) the time complexity of the simulation of nearest neighbor interactions in a 2-dimensional lattice is Θ(n).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the computational power of physical interaction graphs, i.e., the ability of such systems to simulate other physical systems.
the computational power of physical interactions.
the computational power of physical interactions and the complexity of their simulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

for n-partite pair interactions with rational spectrum, the number of time-steps for mutual simulation can be reduced by a constant factor compared to the running time, while for interactions with irrational spectrum the number of time step is at least a linear factor larger.

, while the running time is always polynomial in the number of particles and the number of time layers, the number of time-steps is exponential in the number of qubits for arbitrary interaction graphs, and is at most polynomial for nearest-neighbor interactions in 1D lattices.
for simulating an arbitrary graph of n qubits, the number of time-steps required is at least n.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the simulation of interaction graph Hamiltonians is a hard problem, but that there are efficient algorithms for special cases.
the number of time-steps required to simulate an interaction graph with a given graph code is at least the number of qubits of the graph.
, for a fixed number of time steps, there is a polynomial overhead in the number of qubits, while for a fixed number n of qubits there is an exponential overhead in the number t of time steps.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the time required to simulate an arbitrary interaction graph scales at least as fast as the number of particles.
, while the running time overhead is exponential in n, the number of time-steps required for simulation is polynomial in n.
the computational power of physical interactions is not only determined by the running time overhead, but also by the number of time-steps required to simulate a given interaction graph.
